entities.name: Calippus of Syracuse
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Calippus of Syracuse (born c. 350 BCE in Athens, died c. 301 BCE) was a prominent Greek astronomer and mathematician of the Classical era, celebrated for his significant refinement of the Eudoxian planetary model and the introduction of the 76-year Calippic cycle, a crucial advancement in ancient calendrical astronomy. Operating within the intellectual ferment of late 4th-century BCE Athens, a hub of philosophical and scientific inquiry, Calippus contributed to the sophisticated understanding of celestial mechanics that characterized Hellenistic science, directly influencing major figures like Aristotle and later astronomers. His work addressed the inaccuracies inherent in earlier lunisolar calendars, aiming to synchronize solar and lunar years with greater precision.

Trained under Eudoxus of Cnidus and Aristotle, Calippus inherited and critically evaluated the then-dominant geocentric model of the cosmos. His primary innovation was the modification of Eudoxus's system of homocentric spheres, adding seven additional spheres to better account for the observed motions of Mercury, Venus, Mars, and the Sun, thereby improving the predictive power of the model. More enduringly, in 330 BCE, he proposed the Calippic cycle, a 76-year period designed to reconcile the solar year (approximately 365.25 days) with the lunar month, comprising four Metonic cycles (4 x 19 = 76 years) and incorporating one intercalary month every 19 years. This cycle, equivalent to 27,759 days, was a more accurate approximation of the tropical year than its predecessors, aiming to keep the solstices and equinoxes fixed relative to the calendar date.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Calippus significantly advanced ancient Greek astronomy by refining the Eudoxian model and, critically, by introducing the 76-year Calippic cycle in 330 BCE, which provided a more accurate lunisolar calendar that was foundational for subsequent astronomers like Hipparchus.
